passage:
Monday. Trisha tipped her steel money tin onto the bed and counted the coins: enough for a small keychain for Deepika, who loved anything blue. She skipped the ice lolly at the school gate all week.

Saturday. At the stationery stall she chose a blue keychain with a tiny fish and had it wrapped in newspaper with a ribbon.

Monday after. She handed it to Deepika at recess. Deepika squealed and clipped it onto her bag. Trisha's face split into a smile. She didn't mention that her birthday was next month. When Deepika whispered, "I'll get you something too," Trisha shook her head. "You don't have to. I just wanted to."

qa.q: What did Trisha buy for Deepika?
qa.a: A blue keychain with a tiny fish.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when Deepika clipped the keychain onto her bag?
qa.a: Happy and warm: her face split into a smile.

qa.q: Why does Trisha's reply to Deepika keep the gift from turning into a deal?
qa.a: She says "You don't have to. I just wanted to," so the gift stays about care and not a scoreboard.

qa.q: How might Deepika see the keychain?
qa.a: She squealed and clipped it on right away, so she likely felt loved and delighted, and her whisper shows she wants to give something back.

grounding: A child saves pocket money over days to buy a gift for her best friend, and gives out of care without expecting the same back.

passage: For six weeks, Hafsa dropped her pocket money into an old pencil tin instead of buying samosas after school. On Saturday she walked with Ammi through the crowded lanes of Lajpat Nagar market and chose a sketchbook with a hard green cover, because Indu drew on every scrap of paper she found. At Indu's birthday, Hafsa watched her flip it open and gasp. Warmth spread through Hafsa's chest. Later, Indu's cousin leaned over and whispered, 'What did Indu give you last year?' Hafsa shrugged. 'A pencil, I think. I don't remember.' She really didn't. She was too busy watching Indu draw a fat cat on the very first page.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa keep her pocket money?
What made warmth spread through Hafsa's chest?
qa.a: Seeing Indu gasp over the sketchbook; Hafsa felt happy and loving because the gift suited her friend so well 🤍

qa.q: Why is Hafsa's shrug a healthy answer to the cousin?
qa.a: She wasn't keeping score; she gave out of care, so what Indu gave last year didn't matter to her.

qa.q: How might Indu see the sketchbook?
qa.a: As proof that Hafsa noticed what she loves, since she drew on every scrap of paper she found.

grounding: A girl saves her pocket money for her best friend's gift and gives it from care, not expecting anything back.

passage:
'You spent all your savings on Reena's bracelet?' Didi asked, looking up from her phone.
'Four months of it,' Ira said. 'Did you see her face? She wore it to school every day.'
'And what did she give you on your birthday?'
'She made me a card. And she came.'
'A card. Ira, you should keep a list. Next time, spend only what she spends.'
Ira frowned, twisting her own wrist. 'Then it's not a present, it's a bill.'
Didi laughed. 'Okay, Miss Wise.'
'I liked choosing it. I liked her face. That was the whole thing I wanted.'
Mummy called from the kitchen, 'Your sister's right, you know.'
'Which one?' Didi asked.
'The younger one.'

qa.q: How long had Ira saved for Reena's bracelet?
What does Ira want from giving the bracelet?
qa.a: She feels happy and affectionate; she wanted the joy of choosing it and seeing Reena's face, not anything in return.

qa.q: What could Ira say if someone keeps pushing her to keep a list?
qa.a: Much what she already said: a present is not a bill, and she gave because she cares, not to be paid back.

qa.q: How does Didi see Ira's gift?
qa.a: At first as a bad deal, since Reena only made a card; Didi thinks gifts should be matched.

grounding: A girl explains to her sister that she gave her friend a gift from affection and does not keep score.
